html:
The White Highlands were the cool, fertile uplands of central Kenya reserved for European settlers under British rule, from the early 1900s until 1960.

After the Uganda Railway opened, the government gave settlers, led by figures such as Lord Delamere, large farms on land taken from the Kikuyu, Maasai and others, who were moved to reserves. Africans could not own land there, and many Kikuyu became squatters working on white farms. Kenya became a crown colony in 1920.

Settlers grew coffee, tea, wheat and cattle and had great political power. Land hunger in the crowded reserves and on the farms drove the Mau Mau rising. After independence, much of the land was bought for African farmers or passed to the new elite of Kenya.
sum: The White Highlands were the cool, fertile uplands of central Kenya reserved for European settlers under British rule, from the early 1900s until 1960.
